I'm not sure the "venerate Freud" thing is as correct today as it was in the 1900s. Most psychologists recognize Freud as a pioneer in that he metaphorically framed the subconscious, a thing that is still largely not understood, into a human-accessible model that allowed us to start running tests to see what made us "us." He then indeed began testing against this model, which are largely seen as primitive and incorrect today, but nonetheless still gave us a real-time view of his theories. To whatever degree he's venerated, it's almost entirely due to his theory and very, very little to do with his applied work.

Today's psychiatry is quite a bit different, though with any relatively new field the old fogies often stick with what they know. In much the same way you can choose between an old bonecracker chiropractor and one of these new fancy kids out of 7 years of damn near medical school (and surprisingly get the same damn results), you can still find a Freudian psychiatrist pretty easily.

The field has been shifting toward the Jungian model for a long while now. Like Freud, Jung sought to divide the working parts of the subconscious into terms and functions that could be understood by people, and to create a model through which theories could be tested and an understanding of "us" could be better formulated. His model is much more accessible, focusing less on dreams (though they're still important since man is a visual/symbolic creature by nature), and containing virtually nothing of the sexualization found in Freud's work.

Jung is incredibly easy to read (especially compared to Freud), and is something that the average person might find useful in their lives. I'm not a psychologist or have any interest in the field other than academic, but got curious what the "mumbo jumbo" was about and decided to read it all and find out. Freud sucked. Everything was assholes and dreams being the only important thing ever.

Jung is a beautiful read, and offers a really capable working model of the subconscious. It's still not perfect, but the field is only a few years old. Try this for a start, the first essay in Man and his Symbols is a good read about the importance of dreams and the symbolism inherent in them.
